title: The Last Election, Forever
author: Ashley Frawley
content:
![The Last Election,
Forever](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/AP24301735181091.jpg)

In 1992, a young man named Doug Lain decided to run a goldfish for president.
Dr. Philip B. Carp, a rubber fish, was the candidate of the Random Surrealist
Party, which Lain had also invented. Just old enough to vote in his first
presidential election, Lain was outraged by the Gulf War and a political
system that seemed to offer up candidates with few discernible differences.
The answer to such absurdity was, to him, to become more absurd still. And so
he not only wrote the name of his toy goldfish on the ballot line, but also
campaigned for it, printing pamphlets at Kinko's and urging people to vote
"surrealist."

Lain, now in his fifties, reflects on his youthful stunt in the opening of
_The Last Election,_ a new[
_documentary_](https://fawesome.tv/movies/10827562/the-last-
election?fbclid=IwdGRzaAU3J3ljbGNrBTcnZGV4dG4DYWVtAjExAHBkb2YFc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQMMzUwNjg1NTMxNzI4AAEekyG9b3VCyRLzsw2jkU0_1NmIC9bulbfRr9ZSVkRtj8DUGDDqsqcn2EDWpjQ_aem_yRnebpe1UNRD8VOuPARQoQ&utm_source=social_share&utm_medium=website_fawesometv_copylink&utm_content=video_screen)
from Sublation Media. The idea, he explains, "was to produce a joke so
shocking, funny, or strange that it might somehow change everyone's minds and
start a revolution." Needless to say, the revolution never came, and sifting
through newspaper archives of the time it seems not to have made a blip on the
historical radar. But it was a sign of things to come. Absurd, jokey rejection
of existing institutions has become a familiar mode of political engagement,
as has Lain's youthful disregard for what happens if the rejection succeeds.

_The Last Election_ , centering on the 2024 presidential contest, is equal
parts Louis Theroux, Adam Curtis, and '80s vaporwave. An open-ended
exploration of a particular moment in American political culture, it reveals
the way political rebellion has become the pervasive style of politics, even
as the causes it advances are often unclear. We watch as bored-looking
attendees of the Democratic National Convention say things like, "This is
Obama-era um, politics now. Well, first African American President, male, now
we're fixing to have the first African American female. So… I'm excited" in
unintentionally comedic monotone. Meanwhile, outside the convention, probably
the most articulate interviewee delivers a rousing monologue about the
uselessness of the Democrats in whiteface, while holding a bloodied baby doll
she plans to hang from her genitals. The absurdity that Lain once sought to
highlight with surrealist provocation now seems to need no embellishment.
